A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WEATHER-5K and its forecasting benchmark, despite the changed title and framing. All 26 pages of v1 and 29 pages of v2, including appendices, equations, tables, and figures, support comparison.

before.justification: Tables 2–3 report original forecasting and extreme-event evaluations of nine models. The paper also reports an input-length ablation, dataset analyses, and computational measurements.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds ECMWF-HRES comparisons, ERA5-versus-observation analyses, and weather-event case studies.

M1.justification: No forecasting architecture, objective, or training/inference algorithm is added or revised. V2 expands documentation of dataset preparation without establishing an actual procedure change. Combining TSF and NWP remains a recommendation rather than an implemented method.

E1.justification: The underlying 5,672-station, five-variable, 2014–2023 WEATHER-5K coverage is retained. V2 adds a winter-storm illustration described as evaluation on unseen stations and ERA5 fidelity evaluation including a Chongqing heatwave case. The unseen-station selection is unspecified; MADIS is discussed as future coverage, not actually evaluated.

E2.justification: V2 adds the operational ECMWF-HRES model to both the general forecasting comparison in Table 2 and extreme-event comparison in Table 3, retaining all nine TSF comparators. This introduces a substantively different reference class into the central benchmark; v1 only discussed NWP models.

E3.justification: The main temporal split, 48-hour input, four forecasting horizons, training budget, and MAE/MSE/SEDI definitions remain unchanged. New analyses introduce a three-day storm comparison using RMSE, annual ERA5-versus-observation RMSE, and daily heatwave summaries. These are additional evaluation protocols, not evidence that the retained benchmark was rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds winter-storm and heatwave case studies, ERA5 fidelity analysis, and a cross-model analysis relating temperature MAE to training time and parameter count. The existing input-length ablation and appendix forecast examples are retained. Some annual-pattern panels from v1 Figure 2 are omitted.

E5.justification: Both versions explicitly report single runs and repeat the same assertion of stability across seeds, without adding confidence intervals or significance tests. V2's heatwave shading describes weather-data standard deviations rather than uncertainty across model runs; descriptive means and standard deviations already appear in v1.

E6.justification: V2 adds ECMWF-HRES results, including temperature MSE 8.79 at 120 hours and temperature SEDI 37.4% at the 99.5th-percentile threshold. The nine TSF models' shared per-variable scores in Tables 2–3 are unchanged. Storm, ERA5, heatwave, and parameter-count results are added, while Table 2's overall MAE/MSE entries are removed. Existing appendix training-time and memory values are retained.

T1.justification: The forecasting tensor/mapping formulation and Equation 1 defining the reported extreme-event score are mathematically unchanged. Neither version adds formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or substantive derivations.

C1.justification: V1 primarily contributes a large dataset and comprehensive TSF benchmark. V2 makes assessment of the gap between academic TSF models and operational NWP a central contribution in its title, abstract, and introduction, and adds practical recommendations concerning model complexity. The dataset contribution remains.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations distinguishing short-term TSF competitiveness from longer-term NWP advantages and questioning whether larger models improve forecasting. It expands ERA5 fidelity discussion and refines existing coverage/interpolation caveats with wind-specific imputation risks. V1's explicit dataset-computation-cost limitation is dropped; NWP-assisted bias correction was already recommended.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents ISD field parsing, outlier screening, and decade-wide normalization statistics, and adds model parameter counts in Table 6. Core training settings, hardware, and repository access remain. However, it omits v1's explicit identification of iTransformer and the fixed 72-hour forecast horizon for the retained input-length ablation.

R1.justification: The existing TSF/NWP literature survey is largely retained. V2 adds ECMWF-HRES documentation, Jiao et al. (2021), and ISD–MADIS positioning, and explicitly contrasts its operational-NWP benchmarking with Corrformer's earlier one-day comparisons.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and substantial portions of the introduction are rewritten. Dataset preparation is reorganized into preprocessing, quality control, and post-processing sections, while the findings become four research questions and the standalone ablation subsection disappears. This substantially changes the narrative beyond merely adding results.

P2.justification: V2 adds a storm-comparison figure and processing flowchart, rebuilds the dataset-analysis figure, and combines the redrawn input-length plot with a complexity plot. Tables 2–3 add NWP rows and comparison highlighting; Table 2 loses overall columns. An ISD–MADIS table and parameter rows are added. Appendix forecast images are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: The operational reference in Tables 2–3 and new data-fidelity and complexity analyses make the previously TSF-only benchmark more informative for practical use. However, the newly central ECMWF-HRES comparison lacks forecast-selection/alignment details, the unseen-station setup is unspecified, and retained ablation settings are less fully documented. These tradeoffs support a net improvement in usefulness and interpretation, with limited improvement in empirical rigor.
